d.title: Four derivations of one estimate, and what each is for
d.caption: They give the same β-hat and answer different questions. An interviewer asking 'derive it' wants the second; 'why squared error' wants the fourth; 'why does that one point move the line so much' wants the third. Knowing which view answers which question is most of what fluency here means.

d.title: Five ways to solve it, and when each breaks
d.caption: The normal equation squares the condition number, so it is the first to fail under collinearity — which is why `LinearRegression` does not use it. QR/SVD is the default because it handles rank deficiency by returning the minimum-norm solution instead of raising.

d.title: Six assumptions, and what breaks when each one fails
d.caption: Only two of the six threaten the coefficients themselves; three threaten the **standard errors**, which is why a p-value is only as honest as the assumptions behind it. The last cannot be tested from the data at all — an omitted confounder leaves no residual signature, which is the whole reason causal claims need a design.

d.title: Leverage, outlier, influence — three different things
d.caption: A point can be extreme in x and sit exactly on the line, contributing nothing; or be moderate in x with a large residual and barely move the fit. Influence is the product of the two, which is why Cook's distance is the statistic to read and not either input on its own.

d.title: Why L1 lands on the corner and L2 never does
d.caption: The constraint region's shape decides it. A diamond has corners **on the axes**, and a contour of the squared error is overwhelmingly likely to first touch a convex region at a corner; a circle has no corners, so the solution is shrunk but never exactly zero. The prior view says the same thing: a Laplace prior has a spike at zero, a Gaussian does not.

d.title: Correlated features are where the three penalties part company
d.caption: This is the practical reason to prefer elastic net when you do not know the structure: with a correlated group, ridge shares the weight and stays stable, lasso picks one member **arbitrarily** — so a resample can change which one — and elastic net keeps them together.

d.title: Why a high-degree polynomial fails twice over
d.caption: Two separate failures that arrive together. The statistical one is variance — oscillation between the points. The numerical one is conditioning: the columns x, x², x³ ... are nearly collinear, so the Vandermonde matrix's condition number explodes and the coefficients are solved unreliably even where the fit is fine.

d.title: From odds to the sigmoid, in one line of algebra
d.caption: The sigmoid is not chosen for its shape — it is what you get by asserting that the **log-odds** are linear and then solving for p. That is why logistic regression's coefficients are read as log-odds, and why exponentiating one gives an odds ratio rather than a probability change.

items.desc: log(p / (1 - p)) = Xb — the assumption, stated

items.label: That is the sigmoid
items.desc: derived, not assumed; bounded in (0, 1) by construction

items.label: So a coefficient is a log-odds change
items.desc: and exp(coefficient) is an odds ratio, not a probability

d.title: The sign that flipped: fee and plan in the same model
d.caption: The fee is 7.99, 12.99 or 19.99 **by plan**, plus half a pound of noise — so fee and the plan dummies are nearly the same information. VIF is 77 for fee and 84 for plan_pro. The pair's joint effect is estimated fine; its split between them is arbitrary. Check VIF before reading an odds ratio.

d.title: Family is about the variance; link is about the mean
d.caption: Two independent choices, and conflating them is the usual confusion. The family answers 'how does the spread of y grow with its mean'; the link answers 'on what scale do the effects add up'. A Poisson family with an identity link is legal and occasionally right — here it fitted a minimum mean of −0.75, which is why the log link is the default.

d.title: Choosing the loss is choosing a likelihood
d.caption: Squared error is the Normal likelihood and absolute error is the Laplace — so 'change the loss' and 'change the family' are the same move seen from two sides. Huber caps the gradient, which is exactly what makes contamination unable to drag the fit.
